utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I could remind you, Mr. Abrahams, the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Ms. Kravetz -- oh, I beg your pardon. How could I overlook the fact that Mr. Djurdjic is nearly finished. Carry on, please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will comply with your wishes, but I don't know whether I will be able to do it within the dead-lines that you set.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Abrahams, good afternoon. Let me continue from where we stopped yesterday. In your March 1999 statement, you speak about an incident in the village of Vranic in September 1998. I hope that I corrected all the errors. That should be page 36 in the English version in e-court of P738, that's the exhibit number. Mr. Abrahams -- excellent, well done. At the end of the first paragraph, could you please read the beginning of the sentence: "The commander of the police in Vranic was named Miskovic ..." Have you been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please look at it.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, after you received information from the persons that you interviewed, did you check or were you able to find, to locate, Mr. Miskovic or Mr. Sipka?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the research procedure at that point, but we did not speak with Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did you check whether there was any kind of a police unit in the village of Vranic?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, how did you -- I didn't understand the question. Did we check whether there was police in the village of Vranic or a police station in Vranic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, in this part of your statement you say that Miskovic was the commander of the station in Vranic.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand my statement it says that the villagers claimed that -- no, I'm sorry, you're right. "The villagers claimed that Sipka was involved in Orahovac. The commander of the police in Vranic was named Miskovic" -- yes, that information comes from the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you checked information, whether you checked if there's any kind of police organisation, formal organisation, in Vranic?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall at this point, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, did you go to Suva Reka - and you knew that there was a police station there and an OUP - to check about Milan Sipka, he is mentioned here as a police officer from Suva Reka, just to verify whether this was indeed correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to refer to my notes to tell you exactly where and when I went places in Kosovo, but I can tell you that we repeatedly tried to obtained information from the various police stations around Kosovo and were consistently rejected. We were told that no information would be provided. I cannot tell you for sure without checking my notes whether I approached the Suva Reka station on these dates in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, do you know why you're in The Hague before this Tribunal now?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I had a call from a friend, and he told me that you said 20 times that you had to consult your notes. I didn't count myself but that's what this friend of mine said. You are testifying here for the third time and yet again you tell us that you have to consult your notes to check. So you're not prepared to testify, and when are you going to do it if you have to complete your testimony ? How come also that you are able -- that you have total recall of what the villagers were telling you and you cannot recall what the other side told you and anything that has to do with the side? It says in your statement that Miskovic was the owner of the Bos Hotel. Did you go there and verify this information, who owned this hotel, and did you go there to talk to the owner? Because it was quite close to where you were, Suva Reka, and in fact it's the suburbs, in the outskirts of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of our notes, by me and my colleagues involved in this work, have been submitted to the Prosecutor's office and, to the best of my knowledge, provided to you as Defence. So you are free to consult them. I am more than willing to consult them, but my memory after ten years, having covered in the interim five more wars, is, in fact, hazy when it comes to specific incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. I did not receive any notes of yours from the Prosecution, and I am convinced that the Prosecution would have given it to me if they had been in their possession. But if the Prosecution indeed has them, did you not have an opportunity to go through them in preparation for your testimony? And can we then perhaps postpone your testimony enabling you to consult your notes and then -- so that you can then answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My notes comprise more than ten different notebooks, and that's just mine alone, not the notes of all my colleagues, so I have not had the opportunity to review them in the depth required to answer some of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, now we're no longer dealing with what the Human Rights Watch produced. We're now talking about the statement that you gave to the Prosecution as early as in 1999, so we are not talking about whether you yourself interviewed the witness or not; we are now talking about the statement that you yourself gave in 1999. So this has nothing to do with your research or anything -- or it does, but only because this is a statement that you gave in 1999 to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about what you said to the investigator, and you told us at the beginning of your testimony that this is to the best of your recollection - and you took the solemn oath that you would speak the truth - and that's what I'm asking you about. So I'm not now -- not talking about some work product that you could then say, I did not take part in producing it; I'm talking about your own words, what you yourself said in your statement. Perhaps it's the case that this is not your personal knowledge, what you're saying in the statement. So please do tell me if that is the case, and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything in the statement is a reflection of my personal knowledge and experience and -- including the case you reference here for Vranic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, personal knowledge is a very broad concept. Did you personally interview the villagers of Vranic and what I just read out to you or what you just read, is this the product of your interviews or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- I believe this question has been put already to the witness in several ways, and he has provided the information he's able to provide on this topic. The question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you are putting to the witness passages in one of the statements that he has made. You are then seeking to ask what he did further about a matter. For example, you've referred to a passage that there is a police officer named Sipka from Suva Reka mentioned and that there was a person by the name of Miskovic said to be in charge of the police in Vranic. You're then asking the witness did he personally check or did he personally go to a police station to confirm information, et cetera. That is not something that's in his statement. That is asking him whether he did something about a subject matter that is mentioned in his statement. To that, the witness has said, I am not able to remember clearly whether I did or I did not or whether one of my colleagues may have done so. I would have to check the notes to give you an answer to that. Now, the witness has no way of anticipating what you are going to ask about, and he is trying to remember events that are now many years old, and therefore it would seem to me at least not unreasonable that the witness is not able to remember consequential matters such as those that you have asked about in the questions that I have heard you ask this afternoon. If it is that one of these issues is of such importance, it will be necessary to make some arrangements for the witness to view his notes. We know, he has told us earlier and he reminded us, that there are many volumes, over ten notebooks of his own notes and there are his colleagues' notes which are in addition. Now, the process of going through those will inevitably take some time. For him to be able then to refresh his memory whether a particular action was taken, such as going to a police station to inquire about a particular subject or not. I've spent a little time setting out what I perceive to be the situation. You seem, from what some of the things you have said, to be seeing it a little differently. But if you stand back and think, you may realise that just to be asked now about particular actions so many years ago, it's not surprising that the witness doesn't have a clear personal recollection of each event. Some things, no doubt, he will remember; others things, it is likely, he will not. Now, you must decide, I'm afraid, whether one of these or some of these or all of these subjects are so important that they warrant you asking for the evidence of the witness to be deferred while he checks on a particular issue. I could say that of the matters you've raised so far, it's not apparent to me that any of them are so important as to warrant that time and effort. It must be for you -- you know your case. It must be for you to decide whether it is a matter of great significance or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is not my intention to cause any delays to the examination of this witness to enable him to go through his notes, but I want to lead the Chamber to draw certain conclusions through my cross-examination of this witness. I didn't want to cause any delays. I am clear with your instructions, and I will continue my examinations, and I will be satisfied with the answers that I receive in the hopes that the Trial Chamber will give them proper weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, let us conclude this topic. In this trial, we already clarified who Miskovic was through some witnesses from Suva Reka and what he was, what kind of a job he had; but the reason why I ask you this is because of the statement you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to page 38 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I'm interested in this paragraph that begins with the words: "On the 2nd of November Peter Bouckaert and I spoke with a man in Belgrade JJ ..." My question now is: Am I right if I say that the Defence cannot do anything to verify this source?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man requested anonymity from us; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on to the statement that you gave in 2002, in January. Looking at this statement, I didn't see who actually interviewed you. Could you please tell us how did you conduct this interview on the 24th of January, 2002?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask for the first page to be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'll give you the page reference. That's number 9.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely certain. Again, I could obtain this information, but I believe this statement was taken by two members of the OTP. One is Milbert Shin and the other was Dan Saxon, but I would have to check before being certain of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was this statement taken?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, there was a dual process. It was partially done in The Hague and partially in New York. And if I'm not mistaken, parts of the statement dealing with Kosovo's history were written directly by me in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Now I would like to ask you first of all not to get angry with me, but did you serve in the military? Did you do any national service? Although I know that there is no national service in the USA.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not served in any military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that you don't have any formal military training?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Training as a soldier or formally in the military, no, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And kind of military education in the academia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've studied history, armed -- history of armed conflict and military history as a part of my university studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but did you attend any kind of a military school? Do you have a degree, a post-graduate degree, in military science; or did you attend any other course in this subject outside of your regular studies?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you complete any kind of police schools or police training?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any formal education in constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've taken courses in constitutional law and international law, but I don't have a degree in any of those subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the sphere of criminal law, did you attend any courses, have any training?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Courses only in relation to international humanitarian law and laws of war, war crimes, but not on domestic criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abrahams, could you please tell me, what is the lowest post in the Human Rights Watch organisation, the first one above the interns?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be what we call an associate, which is a largely administrative position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I wasn't specific enough. I'm only talking about the research segment of the Human Rights Watch and what follows after that, drafting of reports, publication of reports, so not the administration, not financial services, nothing of that sort. To cut a long story short, I can see that in 1995 or 1996 you became a researcher. After you completed your traineeship in the Human Rights Watch, what was your job title?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that post?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1995 to 1999 I was researcher, and then I became senior researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you a senior researcher now, or do you have some other job title?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My official title is senior emergencies researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me ask you just one more question: Can you tell us -- can you explain to us what does it mean to edit a report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The editing process is a review and vetting procedure, whereby first the divisional director - in this case the Europe and Central Asia director - and then the programme director review the material for accuracy, consistency, and force of argument. And in this process it is common and normal for the editors or the reviewers to return the document with questions, questions such as: How do you know this? Can we find more proof for this? Are there arguments against this? Did you speak to this person or that person? And finally, the last reviewer is from the legal office, which is looking at it from the perspective of the law in two ways. First is are our arguments appropriately framed with regards to human rights and international humanitarian law; and secondly, will there be legal issues for the organisation regarding libel and other matters related to publication of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you born, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: New York City.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you feel attached to the cultural heritage of the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some aspects of it, yes; to other aspects, less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, where were you in 1974?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time I would have been 7 years old, so in school in New York City.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever read the SFRY constitution?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From cover to cover, no; but sections of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of criteria were you guided by in deciding which portions to read and which not to read?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not an expert on the constitution of the SFRY. My interest in the matter was to understand the context of the Kosovo conflict, and in particular the status of Kosovo within Yugoslavia. I have a basic understanding, but in no sense do I portray myself as an expert on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. I do not want to touch upon the fact whether this really then refers to all the other constitutions in addition to the SFRY constitution to that of Serbia and others that are relevant for our trial.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't perceive a question in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were I to put a question to you now in respect of each and every one of these constitutions, would the answer be the same? That is what I meant. I wanted to avoid putting superfluous questions to you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not an expert in constitutional law or specific constitutions, SFRY's or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you refer to the autonomous province. Do you know when it was that Kosovo and Metohija were conferred the status of an autonomous province?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1974 as well as Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did it enjoy status of an autonomous province before that point?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't believe so, no, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have you read the FNRY constitution dating back to 1963?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the constitutional amendments dating back to 1967, 1968, and 1971?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, What was the constitution which abolished the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My understanding is there were changes to the constitution, but I don't have more detail than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Do you know the difference between a republic and an autonomous province?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general a republic would be on a higher level than an autonomous province with regards to self-setting standards and a degree of independence; but with regards to Yugoslavia, the autonomy granted to Kosovo and Yugoslavia was of a fairly high degree. I know they had representation in the Federal Presidency, they had parliaments, separate legislatures. They were able to set their own policy with regards to education and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that the United States of America constitute a federation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not usually referred to as such, but it is a degree of a federation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The SFRY was also a federation, was it not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the US we have 50-odd states, right, which form part of a federation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many republics did the SFRY have which formed the federation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what period? We're speaking after 1974?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring -- well, let's say after 1974 because that's what you are aware of. How many republics formed the Federation then -- or let me not plague you with this if you can't remember the exact number, let's move on. Were the republics in fact states which formed the Federation of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there were six republics plus the two autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo. And these provinces -- excuse me, these republics did enjoy many of the same rights as the states have in the United States, perhaps not to such a great degree, but they did have their own governments and independent institutions to a degree -- also taking into consideration the dominant role of the communist party at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Right. We don't have time to debate the position of the Human Rights Watch and the communist democracies. But let me ask you this: You keep referring to Kosovo, Metohija, Vojvodina, they were part of which republics? What were they part of in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe both were autonomous provinces within the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your research did you come across a time when for the first time the issue was raised of Kosovo needing to become a republic?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, just re-reading the question. The issue of Kosovo's status has been of -- has been discussed since my first entry into Kosovo in 1995, and it remains a hot topic to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me if you don't remember or you don't know, when was -- when was it that for the first time in your research you came across a demand having been put forward for Kosovo to become a republic?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995 there were Kosovo Albanians who wanted Kosovo to become a republic at that time within Yugoslavia still. Only later did that evolve into independence from Yugoslavia as a whole or now Serbia. But those were individuals. At that time, not aware of formal calls from political groups. That came later -- that came later -- no, I'm sorry -- I stand corrected. I stand corrected. There were calls from 19 -- yes, I apologise. From 1990, from 1990 there were calls for Kosovo's independence. I apologise. If not before, perhaps even 1989/1988. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, What was the enactment which abolished the status of an autonomous province for Kosovo and Metohija and Vojvodina -- or I apologise, you've answered that a while back. I withdraw the question. Let me ask you this: Did the constitution of the Republic of Serbia maintain the equal status of autonomous provinces of Vojvodina on the one hand and Kosovo and Metohija within the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm re-reading because I'm not understanding precisely. At what period are you speaking of? Which Constitution of Serbia, because there were changes to the constitution. If you're asking whether Kosovo and Vojvodina had equal status, then my understanding is yes they did have equal status.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. I'm sure that you as an expert will see the difference that I'm trying to make when I refer to the SFRY constitution and the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia -- or rather, the FRY constitution and the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an expert in human rights and international humanitarian law, but I am not an expert in constitutions. Nevertheless, I do know the difference between the FRY constitution and the Serbian constitution. I just don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abrahams, you say in your statement that on two occasions or perhaps on more occasions you were employed in the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal as an investigator. You spoke to Mr. Rugova, you had an interview with him in November of 2002; am I right -- 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did interview Mr. Rugova for this Tribunal, that is correct. I'd have to check the statement for the precise date, but I believe it was September, October, or November 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before that, as an investigator again, you spoke to Witness Haxhiu Baton and you wrote a statement from him in August 2001?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 24th of January, 2002, you yourself gave a statement as a witness; and the statement we've been discussing is precisely the one, the one that was formed and bears the date of the 24th of February, 2002; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And this statement contains a section where you speak of the historical background of Kosovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: In all your reports or texts whenever you speak of the Republic of Serbia or the Socialist Republic of Serbia and when you want to refer to its autonomous province of Kosovo, you always refer to it only as Kosovo, whereas its proper title was the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. Do you know what Metohija means?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the direct English translation, but I know that it is formally referred to as Kosovo and Metohija in the Serbian language. But our terminology is consistent with the region, whereby we never called Serbia the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, because we never call Yugoslavia the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia but simply Yugoslavia; or not the Republic of Serbia, but Serbia -- for matters of expediency, we shortened the name. And at least "Under Orders" has a short section in the beginning describing our terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which source did you use in drawing the conclusion that in 1989 there was police oppression over someone?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we please have a reference to the passage in this statement that my colleague is referring to, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the historical background. I'll find it now. I didn't think it was in dispute. Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where did you get this from, that on the 23rd of March the Kosovo Assembly, while the Serb police forces were surrounding the area, carried the proposed amendments to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are background matters for our reports. They are context and history. They are not the results of our on-the-ground field investigations which involve interviews with witnesses and examinations of crime scenes. This information is collected from media sources, historical accounts, academic reports, and so on that talk about the history of Kosovo and the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Would your answer be the same in relation to the situation in the field of education as it existed in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To an extent; however, my information about education in Kosovo was buttressed by my personal research in 1996 and the previous visit in 1995 because the conditions for Albanian language education in those years were the same as in 1991 and 1992. So I had historical records plus my own observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rugova and Mr. Haxhiu, did they hold views that were opposite to yours? I'm asking you this because you interviewed them as a researcher -- or as an investigator.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to answer that question. There were many topics that we didn't discuss. They were presenting their views and experiences relevant to the case, at that time mostly the Milosevic trial. And we didn't discuss views or opinions but rather facts and experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is the following piece of information accurate that 16.000 Serb refugees that fled from Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1996 were settled in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt again, but I see my learned colleague is reading from a document. I would appreciate if we could have a reference to which document he is referring to and if it's a witness statement the indication of the page. I would also appreciate it if my learned colleague, when citing the statement, could use the language that's in the statement so that it could be put to the witness in the same terms that's in the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, my notes contain parts of the witness's 2002 statement, Madam Kravetz, and it is the statement that contains these pieces of information that -- and this is something that I thought was not in dispute, that -- the statement in fact does state that in 1996 16.000 Serbs from Bosnia and Croatia settled in Kosovo. I merely wanted to learn what his source was, and that's at page 15 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to check my records. I apologise for that. I do not recall at this moment the source for that information, but I am certain that there was a process of a state policy of trying to re-settle Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as from Albania. There was a Serbian community in Albania, small one, that they tried to re-settle in Kosovo during that time. On the Albanian side I know because I've spoken with some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abrahams, I'd like to know your sources about the forming of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge about the KLA formation comes from various sources, multiple sources. Throughout my time as a researcher in Kosovo, I also encountered and interacted with the Kosovo Liberation Army, as we do with the government and armed forces around the world, armed groups around the world. We communicate and try and obtain information from them and engage in advocacy to improve their behaviour with regards to international humanitarian law. In addition to that, I have been and still am working on a book about the history of Albania, recent history of Albania, not Kosovo but Albania. And in the context of that book, I have also interviewed individuals who were involved in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the issue of the history of the Republic of Albania, you spoke to the members of the KLA to get information on that matter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book has a chapter about Kosovo because it's a modern history, and in that context I interviewed some founders and members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The KLA or FARK?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: KLA, although FARK is mentioned also in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me move on to this brochure that you produced, "Under Orders." Please tell me, it was published in October 2001; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report "Under Orders" was published in October 2001, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that you are listed as the project coordinator?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We talked about the researchers and data gathering. Now I would like to move on to the part -- the chapter where it says that the historical and political background of this report is based on the previous writings of many associates of the Human Rights Watch who started --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, your name is not here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The last portion of the question was not interpreted. The witness did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me read again - and I apologise for reading too fast - the chapter: "The Historical and Political Background" of this report is based on the research and publications of many current and former employees of the Human Rights Watch who started working in Kosovo in 1990. Ken Anderson, Jeri Laber, Ivana Nizich, Vlatka Mihailovic, Julie Mertes, Gordana Igric, and Peter Bouckaert. Your name is not listed here, Mr. Abrahams, among the authors of the historical and political background; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could we please have P741 up on our screens, but I will read.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a brochure of yours. Its title is: "Human Rights Violations in Kosovo" or "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo." And you are listed as the author of the report and some parts were authored by Elizabeth Andersen. Additional research was carried out by Peter Bouckaert, Sahr Muhamed Ally, Suzanne Nossel, and Redmond; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see the page in question, but I take your word for it, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I take your word, Mr. Abrahams. Now this part where it says that it was written by Fred Abrahams, researcher, does it mean that you also carried out the research on which this is based?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I just need to find the document that I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams - that's Exhibit 755 - this is your work. The title is: "Village destroyed, war crimes in Kosovo." Am I right when I say that on page 1, paragraph 2 -- yes, front page just in -- before the abstract you say: "To protect against possible revenge, the Human Rights Watch used initials and pseudonyms for witnesses whose statements appear in this report."

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that reference on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's just above "summary." "In order to protect individuals from possible reprisals ..."

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what it says here?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this report was published, we had reason to fear for the security of the interviewees. I do have the full names of all of the individuals, and I now believe that this fear no longer exists and would be willing to provide the names after a consultation with my notes, so long -- so long as none of those individuals had requested anonymity. And even if they did request anonymity, I am willing to approach them and ask now whether they are willing to lift that condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more thing, just one more question -- I can't find the document, but -- it's: "Kosovo: Rape as a weapon of 'ethnic cleansing.'" Am I right when I say that you authored this report and that two of your associates carried out the research and that it is stated in this document. It's document 386, it's a 65 ter document. But I would like to have the Serbian version too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document, Your Honours, was assigned P00757 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at the end of the document -- or could you please go to page 2 first. Just let me see if it's at the beginning or perhaps it's at the end, page 65. Yes -- no, could we then please have page 65. I'm sorry, sir. That's page 41. My associate has just told me. No, it's not -- well, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, well this was my last question and this document has already been admitted into evidence and it is listed there. So, Mr. Abrahams, I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much for your patience. This completes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have a couple of questions, and I hope we complete before the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, yesterday during the course of cross-examination by my learned colleague you were asked a question relating to events in Kosovo in 1999, and this is at transcript page 4050. Specifically you were asked whether -- why the state of Serbia and the state of Yugoslavia as affluent as it was would shell villages without there being any fighting and that this should happen over and over again, and you responded that you could not comment as to the affluence of the Serbian or Yugoslav state but that you did document a pattern of indiscriminate fire into villages. Could you please explain what you meant when you said yesterday that you had documented a pattern of indiscriminate fire into villages in 1998.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 and early 1999 conducted the five research missions and through interviews with villagers, mostly we were in the villages, the conflict was not at that time in the main cities, villagers told us about a very common practice which was the -- that their homes, their area, would be surrounded by the army and the area would be shelled and the villagers would then flee into the nearby woods or out of the inhabited area, after which the ground forces of the police would -- would enter. So we heard this story consistently. The details were different, but it seemed to us to emerge as a pattern, as a standard operating procedure that we saw again and again. And I can't tell you exactly how many villages, but definitely enough to suggest a pattern which is not to say that there was no KLA presence in those villages. In many of them, there very well may have been. In some of them there definitely were. That's not to say the KLA did not exist and wasn't fighting. In some of those areas they definitely were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. I want to move now to a different topic. Yesterday you were asked about a series of letters of inquiry that were sent by Human Rights Watch in -- on 20th July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 747 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, this is one of the letters that you have seen earlier in your testimony, and it is addressed to the secretary of information, Mr. Aleksandar Vucic. If we could please see page 2 of this letter. It is the cover page. Now if we could scroll down below the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only showed the exhibits that were shown by Ms. Kravetz to the witness. I did not show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned colleague asked extensive questions on these letters of inquiry that were sent on 20th July, 1998. It is true that he showed the letter sent to Mr. Stojiljkovic and also to the Yugoslav Army. This is one of those letters, and I believe the line of questioning that my learned colleague conducted yesterday allows me to show this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be our view as well, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, if we could zoom in below the signature of Ms. Holly Cartner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see there are several entities that are all CC'd. If you could read the list that appears below the signature.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslav secretary of information, Yugoslav minister of the interior, Serbian minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, based on what you're able to see on this letter, would all these persons have received a copy of the letter that had been addressed to the Serbian secretary of information, Mr. Vucic?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain why Human Rights Watch would send a letter to the secretary of information and also CC all these different persons in this type of letter of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For non-governmental organisations such as Human Rights Watch, the secretary of information or Ministry of Information is the common interlocutor. So requests or communications are sent to this office, with the expectation and understanding that they are distributed to the responsible officials within the government, but in this case, apparently, we also sent letters or copies of the letter directly to the ministries concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you were asked several questions yesterday about the mailing list used by Human Rights Watch to distribute its reports, press communiques, and other types of advocacy papers. To the best of your recollection in 1998 and 1999, did this mailing list include the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, the MUP, Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Those or my questions, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions. The Chamber is grateful that you have once again been able to spend time in The Hague and to assist us in this trial. We have your various statements as well as your actual testimony which we will consider in due course. We thank you and of course you may now return to your normal activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we move on to the next witness, there are a number of exhibits -- I believe there were three that were marked for identification at the beginning of this witness's testimony. I just wanted to inquire with the Court whether we would be required to make any further submissions, either orally or in writing, with regard to those exhibits before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think we at the moment see reason for further submissions. We will be considering those submissions and coming down with a decision quite shortly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the question arises whether as a matter of practical convenience we should spend nine minutes with a new witness or adjourn now for the first break and commence with the new witness on our resumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It is our preference if we could adjourn now and commence with the witness after the break. I would like to indicate and I presume Your Honours have seen that Mr. Hannis is in court here today. He's exceptionally here. He will be standing in for Mr. Stamp and will be leading the next witness in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we welcome back, actually, Mr. Hannis. We will therefore adjourn now for half an hour and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness will be Zarko Brakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's what I refer to as a combination witness. We have a 92 ter statement we intend to use, but I also intend to lead him live on some matters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Tom Hannis. I'm a senior trial attorney, a Prosecutor here at The Hague. We haven't met before; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know you dealt some with Mr. Stamp before in preparing for your testimony; but he's not available today, and I'm filling in for him. I'd like to begin by talking about a statement that you gave to the OTP in May of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, with your permission what I'd like to do is I have a binder with B/C/S copies, hard copies, of his statement as well as some of the exhibits I intend to ask him about. I know we'll be using e-court as well, but sometimes I find it quicker to go through some documents if he has a hard copy available. And if there's no objection from Mr. Djurdjic I would ask if the usher could hand this to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That can be done, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, I don't know how you would like to be addressed. Should I call you "mister," or should I call you "general"? I understand you're still active duty in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't mind either way. It's up to you really.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Well I'll call you general. Do you recall having given that statement in May of 2004?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that is 65 ter 05190 for the record. Did you have a chance to read it and review it before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand from my colleague Mr. Stamp that when you did review it, I think earlier this week on Sunday, that you had some changes or corrections that you wished to make; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they are, in fact, only some technical details and mistranslations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can go through those before I ask you to confirm your statement, and I guess the easiest way for me to do this is I will look at the notes that Mr. Stamp made and ask if you can correct that. I know the first corrections you wanted to make had to do with your career details, which are on page 2 of the English. And you wanted to make some corrections concerning the dates. Do you recall what those were now?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 1993 and 1994 I was the commander of the police station in Podujevo. From 1994 through to March of 1995 I was the -- I commanded the PJP unit in Pristina, but under six months I think it was. From 1995 to 2000, head of the police division of the Pristina SUP. Alongside that, from 1997 to 2001 - unless I'm mistaken - I was the commander of the 24th PJP Detachment, which later became the 124th Intervention Brigade. In 2001 deputy chief of the gendarmerie or deputy head, it doesn't make a difference, really. Under promotions and commendations, from 1988 to 1995 I was an independent inspector. I would also like to add that I completed the home affairs secondary school, the police secondary school, and that I was credited with highest marks, and I was the best cadet of my class. And in 1994 I was awarded a pistol from the Ministry of the -- by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In 1996 I received a pecuniary prize from the minister. From February 1999 I became a lieutenant-colonel. I was specially promoted a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say you were specially promoted, what did that mean? Ahead of time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was an early promotion, though not much ahead of what would have been the regular promotion. Let me also add that in 2001 I received a pecuniary reward from the minister of the interior, and in 2003, also from the then-minister of the interior, I received a ducat which is also a sort of an award that is normally given by the minister. And unless I'm mistaken, these are all the corrections I have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I had some notes that there were some additional ones that I'll ask you about. In paragraph 9 of your statement you indicated to Mr. Stamp that there was a change you wanted to make about when the 24th Detachment was increased in size and transformed to the 124th. Do you recall what that was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the statement says that the 24th Detachment of the PJP increased in size in 1998 to deal with the developing security crisis in Kosovo, and with this increase it became known as the 124th Intervention Brigade. The only comment I made was that I do not think that this was the reason behind this change. It -- either what we were discussing was misconstrued or what I wanted to say was misinterpreted. In page -- in paragraph 11 we also found a linguistic error. It says OPG. In Serbian that means the operational sweep group, whereas I was told that in the English translation, the way it is written, it says something else; and I think that what I meant or had in mind was much better. I think in English it was some sort of a clean-up that was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think what you had indicated was that in the B/C/S the Serbian word for sweep is not included, but I will tell you that in the English version the OPG is translated as operational sweep groups. So it seems like the English is correct and there was just a Serbian word missing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not. You see, there's a difference. A clean-up operation implies quite something else than the sweep operation implies. A sweep operation is an operation aimed at searching an area. A clean-up means something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's nothing in the English about clean-up. It only has sweep. Is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I was -- I received in the interpretation that Mr. Stamp [sic] had said operational search groups or investigating groups. I think that they might have caused the problem. The other term "ciscenje" or clean-up was also used. I know what the OPG means in Serbian. I don't know what the English translation should be, but definitely not -- it should not involve investigation or anything of the sort, as was said that Mr. Stamp [sic] had referred to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I don't know whether the matter's any clearer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I think I understand. The English word is "sweep" and I think that's consistent with what the witness and Mr. Djurdjic believe it should be, and I -- that's my position. And I would also indicate that Mr. Stamp is not here, and Mr. Stamp hasn't said anything yet today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the moment we'll take it in English as sweep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is there anything else in the statement that you wanted to change or bring attention to the Judges today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, no, I don't think that there's anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that we will be discussing these matters in the course of my testimony, and then we might come across certain issues that can be left as they are at present but will be explained in our discussions; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. One point I wanted to make now, though, are you satisfied and can you confirm to the Court that with those changes that we just went through that your written statement is accurate and that you would answer the questions that were put to you then in the same way today if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes. Again, as I said, with certain explanations because some of the statements herein are quite short and perhaps require additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With that, Your Honour, I would like to tender 5190 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00759, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand it's the procedure, Your Honour, in this court at this time for me to read a brief summary of what the statement is about, if I may do so. Thank you. In 1999 the witness was the commander of the 24th PJP Detachment, later the 124th Intervention Brigade, and the head of the police department of the Pristina SUP. The witness gives an overview of the MUP structure in Kosovo. He describes the organisational structure of PJP units, describing their uniforms, equipment, modalities of intervention, and operations, with a particular focus on the 24th Detachment, then 124th Intervention Brigade. He also describes how anti-terrorist operations were conducted in 1999, whereby the PJP units involved were under the operational command of the VJ for the specific operation. He specifies that in general all anti-terrorist operations were planned by the VJ which would issue the combat orders and plan of the operation. He describes the coordination between the VJ and the MUP, PJP, for combat operations. The witness occasionally participated to meetings of the MUP staff in Kosovo and will testify to visits to Kosovo by General Obrad Stevanovic and General Vlastimir Djordjevic in 1999. He will also testify to the VJ headquarter in the Grand Hotel in Pristina during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, if I may, can you tell us -- we have your written statement, the Judges have that information, so I'm going to go to some particular points. What position did you hold in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: If you'll allow me to just make two points before answering your question because this may be important for my subsequent testimony. It is common knowledge that the events that I am supposed to testify about today happened more than ten years ago. The documentation that I had and which could have proved useful to me for my preparation for today perished in the bombing of the Secretariat of the Interior in Pristina where I used to work. I think the bombing happened on the 29th of March, 1999. In the meantime, I was engaged in a similar assignment, though not equal in scale or scope. I wish to tell you that I will do my best to recall all the relevant events and incidents that will be of interest for the Chamber. Can you please repeat your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us what position you held within the MUP beginning from 1998.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999, I was the chief of the police department of the Pristina Secretariat of the Interior. As I said, concurrently I held the position of a commander of what was at the time the 124th Intervention Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: The same as above. If we're talking about the early 1998, I was the commander of the 24th Detachment unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you explain for us what was the 24th PJP Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 24th PJP Detachment was one of the units, one of the special police units of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. It was one of several PJP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the 24th was located in Pristina, Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not stationed in Pristina, rather, it was composed of members of the police from the Secretariat of the Interior from the area of Kosovo. It was not a standing unit. It was an ad hoc unit composed of members of the regular police forces which would when necessary come together and form the ad hoc 24th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1998 approximately how many members were there in the 24th PJP Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly, roughly 850. Again, I have to emphasize that I can't be quite precise in the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. I will take it that for numbers and dates that sometimes you may just be giving us your best approximation because we're talking about ten years ago. Of those 800 or 850, approximately, PJP members, do you have an idea of what percentage of them came from your Pristina SUP? Was it 10 per cent? 20 per cent? Can you give us any help with that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the Pristina Secretariat of the Interior, there were two companies of the total of eight companies. So seven Secretariat of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija, they existed there, and six provided one company and the Pristina secretariat provided two companies because it was the largest one. And now I can't really give you the percentage in regarding the regular standing personnel strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you were the commander of the 24th Detachment in 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges when you were made the commander and by whom, how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I am not mistaken, if my memory serves me right, I was appointed the commander of this detachment in 1997. I was preceded by my late colleague Jovica Milancic. And when he died a few months later, the then-chief of the Pristina SUP - I think it was Djordja Keric - recommended that I should be appointed detachment commander because the Pristina Secretariat of the Interior was the secretariat from whose ranks commanders were appointed to the post of -- as detachment commanders. And this is why I was put on the personnel list because in order to be a member or an officer in the PJP, you didn't have to have a written decision to that effect because there was a decision to the defect that once you were put on the establishment list you became a member. I think it was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to becoming named the commander, had you been just a regular member of the PJP; and if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I didn't really understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you got named the commander in 1997, had you been just a regular PJP member not holding a command position; and if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a member of the PJP from the very time when it was established in 1993 I think, but between 1995 and 1997 I was not a member, but in the period before that I was, from 1993 in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. One thing I'm not clear on is as commander of the PJP, the 24th Detachment, I understand that was an ad hoc body, you also had your regular job in the Pristina SUP as head of the police department; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in your job in the Pristina SUP as head of the police department, who was your boss, your immediate superior, is that the chief of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the secretariat where I was the chief of the department, my superior was the chief of the secretariat. And the secretariat in Pristina - let's take that as an example - had about 13 departments. So I was one of the 13 department chiefs from various segments. And let me add here, while I was the detachment commander, I could not have at the same time served as the department chief. It's logical. So it was physically impossible for me to perform both those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So how did that work? When you became detachment commander you didn't do any work anymore as head of the police department during that time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that the 24th Detachment was an ad hoc unit. It was not a standing unit, and it performed tasks from that sphere. So when I did jobs that had to do with the 24th Detachment, I did not at the same time act as the department chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand now. So -- but when the 24th was not actively engaged in anything, then you were doing your regular job; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In 1998, the 24th PJP detachment became the 124th Intervention Brigade. Do you recall approximately when that occurred? I think we'll look at a document in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was in June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1998 and 1999 can you tell us who was the head of the SUP in Pristina. I know it changed. There was at least one or two changes during that time, but can you tell us beginning in 1998 who was the chief of the Pristina SUP and then who it was by the end of 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Pristina SUP was Colonel Bosko Petric. If my memory serves me right, I think that in April it was Colonel Bogoljub Janicevic who was appointed the chief. Before that he served as the chief of the Urosevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why Colonel Petric was replaced?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not the nature of my job to know that at the time, but I did not see this as his removal from office because he was sent from the Uzice secretariat there, he was seconded there. And once the -- his secondment expired, he simply went back to his original job. I think there is even a limitation under the law for the time that one can stay away from one's original unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you very much. The witness responded, but I do not like the way that Mr. Hannis is phrasing his questions because the witness never did say that Colonel Petric was removed from office. And the way that question was asked was: "Do you know why Colonel Petric was removed from office in April," and I think these are very important issues and this is not just a question of linguistic nuance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, my question was: "Do you know Colonel Petric was replaced?" The witness's statement paragraph 1 says: "... Colonel Bosko Petric until the end of April 1999 when he was replaced ..." I'm using the exact words in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, when you were acting as commander of the PJP detachment and later the intervention brigade, in that role, when it was active and engaged, who was your superior? Who did you report to for purposes of activities of the PJP unit?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: What period are you talking about, and what tasks do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, 1998 and 1999 is the time-period, and I'm talking about any time when the PJP was formed to carry out a task so that you would be working as detachment commander instead of working at your regular job as head of the police department.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1998 and 1999 we were mostly deployed in Kosovo and Metohija. My superior command, so to speak, at that time as regards those activities was the MUP staff which was established in Pristina, so for those activities, because according to a decision, the relevant decision, they were responsible for that, and they were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a particular individual in the MUP staff that you were responsible to or that you reported to concerning activities of your PJP unit?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're talking about anti-terrorist actions that we conducted in that period, I said that we carried out those missions for the most part in accordance with the pre-existing plans that we received, and we acted in accordance with those plans. So as far as I know, the format, the contents, and all the other aspects of those plans, I think that it was all done and produced by the military command. And as regards the reporting following those actions, the reports were submitted by the command of the unit that I was in the field with and I was subordinate - I think that's the correct term. And now, as for notification, I informed the MUP staff whenever somebody called to inquire about the goings-on, what was happening, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who would that MUP staff member be? Was it always the same person or different people?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not always the same person. It would be some officer from the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the names of those persons from the MUP staff that you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was Dusko Adamovic, Miroslav Mijatovic -- well, I can't now recall, but probably other people too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've described the PJP unit that you commanded as being an ad hoc body that was not a standing unit that came together and got active as needed. Can you explain to the Judges the process, how that worked. Who decided when your detachment or brigade was going to be needed? Do you know who made that decision and -- well, answer that first, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who planned those activities. I assume -- well, since the documents were produced in terms of their format and contents in the way that it was done in the military; so I assume that the information about the MUP units, the independent MUP units, was submitted by somebody from the staff. Now, as for my unit, I couldn't really give you an answer. It was probably somebody -- well, in accordance with the procedure that I've already outlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how would you become informed that your unit was going to be required to do a task? Wasn't there somebody in MUP who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually we would receive our task and the documents that we needed to carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was either some of the officers from the staff or we would receive this in the field at those briefings that we had together with the army personnel in the course of the preparations for the task. But from the beginning of the war, the whole procedure became more complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what way did it become more complex with the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it became more complex because the building where the staff headquarters was located, the secretariat headquarters, was hit by bombs and the staff was moving all the time. So when we were summoned to attend a meeting, we never knew where the meeting would be held. We went then to the secretariat headquarters, took the documents, and then we went to talk to the military people, and we would do all the preparations that were necessary, including reconnaissance and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I assume that in 1999 after March 24th when the bombing started, that your PJP or your intervention brigade was engaged full time, every day, throughout the end of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what percentage of the time was your PJP unit active during the months of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may be allowed to say this, I said that 124th Intervention Brigade consisted of eight companies, and it was never deployed in its full composition, at full strength, the eight companies. Mostly there would be only four or five companies from the Pristina secretariat, Urosevac, and Gnjilane secretariats, and maybe a company here and there that was unengaged at the time or that was based in the territory where the mission was to be carried out. Other companies were used by other PJP detachments, so one or two companies. So at that time, I did not know whether they were actually engaged in any kind of mission because they were not under any obligation to report to me. They performed their tasks in accordance with the plans that they had received. So I was only in charge of coordinating the companies that were under the plan envisaged as participating in a mission and for the specific mission that I was appointed the head of the unit for. So I could not give you a percentage. But I assume that there were quite a few occasions when the unit was engaged and deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you can help me out, I'm a little unclear then about your role as commander of the 124th Intervention Brigade. I think you told us before there were -- is it correct there were eight companies in the 124th Brigade in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as commander were you the commander of all eight companies?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of all those eight companies, but when only some of the companies were engaged to perform a task, then I commanded only those companies that were performing that task. I was not a commander of the companies that were not engaged under me but were engaged in tasks to be performed by other PJP detachments or the military. PJP is a specific kind of unit because it is an ad hoc unit. There is an establishment structure, but that doesn't mean that at any given time all its members have to be deployed or engaged. But it depends on the actual needs based on the task, the specific task. So if I was designated as the person in charge of a certain task or mission, then I commanded the companies that were designated as being deployed to perform it. I don't know if I was clear. So this was not like a standing unit in the military with the permanent command and the permanent composition and everything that goes with it. It was an ad hoc unit which did have its accomplishment and it was used for each specific task in the strength that was necessary to actually perform that task. The same went for all the PJP detachments, not just the unit that was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me follow-up to be sure I'm understanding.
