You had eight companies in your brigade and say, because of the situation in Kosovo in April 1999, two of your companies were requested to help the VJ in Pec and two of your companies were requested to help in Suva Reka, how did that work? Are you still the commander of those companies, or is their command delegated to someone else? Can you explain that if you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the command was transferred to whoever they were carrying out the task with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that when there were joint operations performed by the VJ and the MUP, that - according to your statement - the MUP unit was subordinated for the purpose of that combat task or action; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But do you know who decided when two companies of your brigade were going to be sent somewhere else for a task? Did you have any say in that or was that done by somebody higher in the MUP or by the VJ? How did that happen? Who got to choose?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not decide. Now, I couldn't really tell you who got to choose, but I assume that it was done by somebody in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how did you become aware that two of your companies were going to be going to Pec next week to help the VJ? Did you receive a document or did somebody from the MUP staff call you? Did somebody from the company say, Hey, Boss, we're going to Pec? How do you find out?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't really understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. If you're the brigade commander, the overall commander of these eight companies, if it came about that two companies were going to be required to go help with a specific task or action and assist the VJ, for example, in Pec, how did you find out about that? Did somebody first ask you, Can you loan us two units? Or did your boss say, You need to send two of your companies there? Or did you find out once your two companies had arrived in Pec and say, Hey Boss, the VJ needs us over here? How did that work? There must have been a system in place.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Normally one company was engaged only. Only in very rare cases were two companies engaged because they were distributed or present along the various secretariats. So if there was need for one company to be deployed to, let's say, Pec, then that one company would be dispatched from the secretariat in Pec, rather than having another unit come in from a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So are you telling me that your eight companies in Pristina never operated outside the area of Pristina municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm under the impression that you misunderstood me. There weren't eight companies in Pristina. There were two companies in Pristina only. My feeling was that you phrased your question differently. I said at the outset that each secretariat had one company. There's the Kosovska Mitrovica; then Pec; third, Djakovica; fourth, Prizren; fifth, Urosevac; sixth, Gnjilane; and there were two companies present in the secretariat in Pristina. Had there been a need to engage one company for the purposes of the area of Pec, then the company stationed with the Pec secretariat would have been the one to be deployed. I don't know if I was clear enough this time, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I do now, and you're right, I misunderstood or I had forgotten what you told me when I first asked my question. But in light of what you've said just now, of those eight companies, the two in Pristina, the others in the various municipalities you described, weren't there times during the war, for example, where the needs were such that a particular PJP company was called upon to operate outside its home municipality, if you will?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there probably were. However, I wouldn't be able to give you a specific example. I suppose that there probably were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But as you sit here right now, you can't remember that ever happening?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall a specific instance, but I presume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we'll come back to that when we look at some of the documents. And I would like to look at one document right now. This is 65 ter number 01252. And, General, for you in the binder it's the tab marked number 25, if you could have a look at that. And my English translation indicates this is a decision on the composition of the staff, leaders and members of the staff of the MUP for Kosovo and Metohija. The date is not clear on my copy. I think it's May 11th, 1998, and it appears to bear the signature and stamp of General Djordjevic. Have you seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see item number 4 lists you -- I guess your grade level at the time was major. It says: "Major Zarko Brakovic, chief of the police department of the SUP Pristina, as the assistant staff leader for police affairs." Were you ever told that you had been named a member of the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me that. My view is that the composition of the staff was somewhat different based on what I know from my work in reality. Nobody informed me of me holding this position, nor did I ever feel I was discharging it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll come to more about that in a minute. In your witness statement, which is now Exhibit P759, in paragraph 5 you said: "By virtue of my position as commander of the 24th Detachment of the PJP and the 124th Intervention Brigade, I was a member of the MUP staff for Kosovo until June 1998 ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. If the Trial Chamber is interested, I can offer an explanation of the principle underlying this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: When my predecessor, the late Milacic, was the commander of the 24th Detachment before my time, he was appointed assistant leader of the MUP staff alongside the other position. My guess is that when I replaced him I automatically became a member of the staff, and that was between 1997 and 1998, unless I'm mistaken. So what I said there was that I was -- I held that position on paper, but I did not effectively participate in the work of the staff, save for having attended several meetings. I had no other role to play there. That was in 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement you say you held that position on the staff until June 1998. What happened in June 1998 that changed that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I was never the one to be appointed to any position. It was in somebody else's hands, and I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how did you know that you weren't on the staff anymore? Did somebody tell you, Mr. Brakovic, don't come to the staff meetings anymore? How did you find out?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I found out because some other individuals appeared in the staff and carried out the duties that were defined for them. I can't remember whether it was somebody from the staff who told me as much. I don't remember, but I suppose that that's how I learnt, somebody told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was that told you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I told you in my answer there I can't remember. There's a possibility that it might have happened either way, that's why I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Related to that let me show you another document and we'll come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, I want to tender this but perhaps I need to talk about the next one first. Can we have a look at exhibit in evidence P57.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is the next tab for you, General, it's tab 26. And this is dated the 16th of June, 1998, entitled: "Decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism." Have you seen that document before today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, during the preparation for my testimony in the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade. And I was preparing for my testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the first time you'd ever seen it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who in the ministry showed that to you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in reference to what I said about my preparation for the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody showed it to me. I asked to be given access to certain documents that might assist me in providing a relevant testimony today. Among others, this decision was in the documents I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how did you phrase your request? What documents did you ask for?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask for any specific documents. I asked to be given access to the archives, and I was. Subsequently, I sought certain documents that were relevant for me, and they were made available to me in photocopies -- or rather, on a CD, and I have them. But I don't think I have this particular decision. It wasn't relevant. So I don't have it. I only saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Well -- so you saw this one but you didn't see the previous one we looked at where it has your name as being appointed to the staff; is that right? Nobody showed you that one?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. From what you know about the MUP staff in June 1998 and in -- through the rest of the year into 1999, are the people listed here in P57, the document at tab 26 in your binder, the people who were members of the MUP staff based on what you saw and heard and knew?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. A number of them were and a number weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us which ones were to the best of your memory and knowledge? General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: David Gajic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: As for David Gajic, I saw that he be -- that he was an official member of the staff, I saw that for the first time in this particular document. I had seen him at meetings, but I didn't know in what capacity he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand he was -- he was on the state security side of the MUP, right, not the public security side?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know Zivko Trajkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he was the head of the SAJ units at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could look at the last page, item number 6, above the minister's name and signature, if you could read that paragraph and -- you don't have to read it out loud. Just read it to yourself. Let me know when you've finished.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in essence the minister seems to be saying this decision, MP 57, appointing a staff for the suppression of terrorism, is a decision that supersedes, overrules, takes the place of certain other decisions that aren't going to be valid anymore. One of those, the last one listed, is strictly confidential number 1206/98-2 of 11 June 1998, and I would suggest to you that that number refers to 01252 at tab 25 in your binder, where you're named as being a member of a staff in -- a MUP staff in Pristina. I don't know what you can see on your B/C/S copy regarding the number and date. I know it's rather blurry, but would you agree with me that that's what it seems to refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't find either the number or the date here. I can only see the titles. It is possible that this was the case, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think on -- on the one from General Djordjevic in the lower left near his signature do you see what appears to be a number and date although part of it may be too light to read, can you see a partial number or date there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that it says 206 here and then 110, which is probably a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that would explain perhaps why you never were told you were made a member of the staff because this decision on the 11th of June, 1998, was overridden on the 16th of June, 1998, by the minister's order; does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Presumably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, now I would tender 1252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am absolutely in agreement with the fact that this document is relevant for the trial and that it has to be admitted into evidence; however, I place an objection with regard to the criteria. The witness is not familiar with the document. He said that he had just seen it -- he has just seen it for the first time, and the document is supposed to be tendered through the witness. I don't think that this should be the way it should be done, but if this is indeed the case and if the document is going to be introduced through the witness in this way, then I only ask that this same practice be employed throughout the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps it would assist if I ask a couple more questions. I don't want to be hoist by my own petard and then be faced by having too low a standard for the admission of evidence later on when I may be in the position of trying to object to something that Mr. Djurdjic wants to put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your submission briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to ask the witness a couple more questions concerning the document I'm asking in terms of form and regularity and similar to others that he may have seen of a like nature. And I don't know if Your Honours have the copy of the B/C/S original to look for yourself to see what parts of the number and date on that that you may determine whether it could be the same document that's referred to in P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have what is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the date is absolutely correct. I want to say this to my learned friend, Mr. Hannis. And we do have a document in e-court which is a much better copy of this one. The date is correct. The date on which this document supersedes the earlier documents, referring to the staff. That's something that's true. The date is definitely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what I wanted Your Honours to look at is not the one that's on the screen. The one on the screen makes reference in the English to number 1206/98-2 of 11 June 1998, but I need you to look at 1252 at the B/C/S to see if that number appears to be that same number and that date of 11 June. And it's in the lower left directly across from the stamp and signature. And I would argue to Your Honours that given the contents of the document, what's described in Minister Stojiljkovic's order about what he's superseding, it makes sense. He's creating a MUP staff for suppression of terrorism, and he's directing that that order supersede an earlier one. This earlier one is General Djordjevic's order creating a MUP staff, not particularly for the suppression of terrorism but a MUP staff. Given the timing, the contents of the two documents, I think logic dictates even though you cannot -- at least I cannot read every single digit in the number and date, I think there's enough for you to be satisfied that it can be admitted and considered with other evidence throughout the course of the trial to give it whatever final weight you deem appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We now have on the screen the electronic copy of the document that you have shown to the witness I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it the case that there is another form in e-court of this same order which is more legible? Which is what I understand Mr. Djurdjic to be saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's the best I've ever seen. If there's a better one, I would be happy to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There certainly is one in my possession. I don't know if there's one in e-court. I do have one which is a much better copy. We do not dispute the date. It is the 11th of June, 1998, and the reference number is the one that was stated here, and it was signed by Mr. Djordjevic. And let me just state that I do not contest the date. What I was referring to is that I wanted both sides to have to follow the same criteria for admission of evidence. That's what I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to locate a better version of this decision. I don't know if I can do it in the next three days or five days, depending on how busy I will be, but I will definitely locate the copy that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the Chamber does try to be consistent with the admission of evidence. The receipt of official documents is often something that can be undertaken on the basis of the document's apparent regularity, its dating, its apparent signature, its -- the stamp that is often on it, and so forth, or the source from which the document was obtained. And those matters are weighed. Sometimes they will be sufficient, sometimes they will not be. As I understand Mr. Djurdjic, Mr. Hannis, he does not object to the admission of this document, accepting the correctness of the date, although on the copy of the screen -- that is on the screen it is incomplete or indistinct. But he accepts that it is the correct document. Therefore, by consent we could receive this without any further ado.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would request that you do that, Your Honour, and I appreciate Mr. Djurdjic's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 01252, Your Honours, would be assigned P00760.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, I understand this is the time you take your first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second break I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. First for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume then at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I would like next to show you an exhibit, it's tab number 13 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, this is Exhibit P257 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you'll see that's a decision on the formation of the 124th Intervention Brigade of the PJP, signed by Minister Stojiljkovic on the 18th of June, 1998. Have you seen that document before today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When was the first time you saw it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most logically it was in a time-period that followed the issuing of this decision -- well, I couldn't really tell you when it was, what date, but that is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see in item 1 that the 124th was to be formed by integrating the 24th PJP Detachment and the Mechanised Police Brigade in Pristina. Can you tell me what was the Mechanised Police Brigade in 1998 in Pristina? How big a unit was that and what kind of equipment did it have?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as indicated here, this unit was set up from the mechanised brigade and the 24th Detachment of the Pristina police. The mechanised brigade of the police was set up in the 1980s, if my memory serves me right - this is when I began my service in the police - in the joint detachment of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, if I'm not mistaken. With time its strength was reduced. So in 1994 when, or rather, 1995 - I am sorry, it slipped my mind temporarily - when I was appointed the chief of the department of the interior in the secretariat in 1995 the mechanised brigade for all intents and purposes did not exist as an organised unit. So before that and after it was established, it had a lower-rank unit in each of the secretariats. I don't know what that unit was called. So after 1995 - I can say that with certainty - it did not exist as an organised unit but the equipment that was left behind that used to belong to the mechanised brigade was given to the secretariats for their use. And this is what happened with the element of that unit in Pristina. Technically or formally this segment that was in Pristina was covered by us from the secretariat, and there was a person who was the commander of the brigade; he worked with me in the department of the interior that I was the chief of. But that was not an active-duty unit so to speak. But the secretariats were given the equipment for their use, they were supposed to maintain it, and use it as they saw fit. The secretariat had a certain number of armoured vehicles. There were some armoured personnel carriers, tracked vehicles, and there were also some wheeled armoured vehicles to be quite precise. When the unit was set up - now I'm talking about the 124th Intervention Brigade - the mechanised unit, which was part of that mechanised brigade which, as I said, was in the secretariat so it didn't exist for all intents and purposes - the equipment was taken from the secretariats to meet the needs of the PJP units that also belonged to those secretariats. As I said, there was several armoured personnel carriers, but because those armed personnel carriers were out of order that they could not be used, they didn't -- they were not taken over, they just remained there. And the wheeled armoured vehicles, the BOVs, armoured fighting vehicles, were taken over. And in the establishment list of the 124th Brigade they were included there on the list, they became part of it. I don't know whether I made myself clear because I was quite extensive, but the mechanised brigade did not exist as an organised unit. There was just the equipment that belonged to the mechanised brigade in the secretariat. So when this decision was issued, the equipment was taken over and given to the PJP companies and the secretariats for their use. So that would be it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry. So it did not have a permanent composition. So these were not people who were members of that unit and they performed only tasks that were given to that unit. That was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My next question has a link to your statement. In paragraph 9 of your original statement you talked about the PJP increasing in size in 1998 to deal with the developing security crisis in Kosovo. And with this increase became known as the 124th. But at the beginning today you said you wanted to change that paragraph and you wanted it to reflect that you didn't know why the PJP increased in size and became -- and the 24th became the 124th. Would you look at paragraph 2. It says: "The tasks and duties of the intervention brigade are focused on security, the suppression of terrorism, and other special complex security tasks within the jurisdiction of the MUP and protection of the security of the republic and its citizens." Now, remember, this document is dated the 18th of June. We saw that two days before, on the 16th of June, Minister Stojiljkovic had created a MUP staff in Kosovo for the suppression of terrorism. Reading those two things together, doesn't that refresh your memory that this was being done because the security problem in Kosovo was indeed getting worse in June 1998. That's why the PJP got bigger, right, to deal with this increasing problem?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I really did not draw this conclusion. That was not my impression. But now when you maybe establish a link between the dates, perhaps yes; but at the time, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Have a look at the next paragraph. "Putting the intervention brigade on stand-by, assembly, and engagement for the task in paragraph 1 shall be done on the orders of the minister and on his authorisation of the chief of the public security department." That sounds like the people who decided about when the intervention brigade was going to be put on stand-by or gathered together or engaged for tasks was a decision by the minister, or if he delegated it to the chief of public security, General Djordjevic. Does that refresh your memory about who made the decisions about when the PJP intervention brigade was going to be used?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me remind the Trial Chamber that what we talked about, the readiness and the gathering of the brigade personnel, the same thing went for all the PJP detachments. In the decision to form PJPs, there is the same provision but it pertains to all the other PJP units. And in this sense I really don't see a difference. This decision pertains only to the 124th Brigade. I assume that this is why it's listed here, but otherwise the same rule was valid for all the other PJP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it sounds like if there was an order from the minister or General Djordjevic to you as a PJP brigade commander to stand-by or to assemble or to engage, you would have had to follow that order; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're talking about 1998 and 1999, that is true, but in that period, the unit was used through the staff. It was the staff that decided how to use the unit. It was not done directly by the persons that were mentioned. It was only the MUP staff that could order the use of the unit for tasks that were defined in the decision to establish the staff. So what do I want to say? This is what it says here, but in practice it was different. It was only the staff that could decide how to use the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to whom was the staff responsible, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with the decision that we have just seen, it was responsible to the minister, if I understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your preparation for testimony, do you recall Mr. Stamp showing you a number of documents signed by General Djordjevic deploying PJP detachments or units to Kosovo in 1998 and 1999? Do you recall seeing those?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was a dispatch. That's what we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There were several of those; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, could you look at paragraph 7. My English translation reads: "When the intervention brigade is standing by, assembled or engaged for special security task as in item 2 or training in item 3 of this decision, the commander and the commanders of the companies, platoons, and detachments shall have the duties and powers of leaders of corresponding organisational units of the ministry, that is, of the police units in these organisational units." Can you explain that for me. I have a hard time understanding this phrase about organisational units of the ministry. What does this mean about your power as a commander of this brigade? Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this paragraph - and I'm no lawyer - this is the way I see it. Since the unit is not a permanent unit, it is not composed of people who do no other job but that, it is composed of police officers who are -- who have a decision assigning them to regular duties. Now, members of the unit remain in the posts that they were assigned to in accordance with the decisions, their regular posts, and they have the duties and rights of the leaders of appropriate units of the ministry. This is a reference to those decisions, which means that if a platoon in a company from the secretariat in Kosovska Mitrovica, now the commander of that platoon is the commander or an officer from a police station in Kosovska Mitrovica. The personnel in that platoon are officers from that police station. So this platoon commander is their commanding officer in their regular duties and in those extraordinary duties that they have to perform. So this is the reference to that. So when they are deployed in the PJP doing PJP tasks, all the responsibility in terms of their performance, discipline, and so on, those commanding officers are duty-bound to -- they have the authority to deal with their subordinates in the manner that I have already explained. I don't know if I have made myself clear. So the platoon commander was duty-bound to take care of his members, personnel, in any way in terms of performing their tasks and disciplinary measures and so on. Why? Because disciplinary responsibility was not imposed at the level of the unit, but at the level of their decisions assigning them to their regular posts. So to give you an example -- so if somebody failed to obey an order issued by the platoon commander, the platoon commander could institute disciplinary proceedings against this person, but disciplinary proceedings could only be instituted in the original police station, not in the PJP, if you understand what I'm saying, because disciplinary responsibility was something that was taken care of in the original unit. So I think that all of this, what you said about authority and the take-over of command, that the same applied to that. I apologise in advance if I didn't make myself clear, but if I haven't made myself clear perhaps you can ask some follow-up questions and then I will be able to rephrase my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I need to -- I thought I was following you and then you got on the specific topic of discipline and you lost me at a turn. If a PJP policeman, say Officer Markovic, in the PJP company that's part of your brigade is from Pristina, he's from the Pristina SUP in a PJP company, he's out doing a PJP task, and he refuses to obey an order or commits some other disciplinary offence, who would have an authority to discipline him? Is it only his platoon commander or could it go all the way up to you as brigade commander? Or does it go to the chief of the SUP? Who has the ultimate authority to decide on discipline in that situation?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this specific case, the commander of the platoon where police officer Markovic is serving who works together with him in the police station, would file a disciplinary report to the commander of that police station; and there is a disciplinary court within the secretariat, it's an independent institution, so to speak, which would then deal with the disciplinary report and decide how to punish this police officer Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then you as brigade commander department have any disciplinary authority over the PJP members engaged in PJP activities? It goes to the SUP chief no matter what; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: More or less. I did not have the power to take specific measures. I could tell the platoon commander to notify the commander of the police station to file a disciplinary report, and then the normal procedure would follow. But I couldn't punish that person because the system of responsibility in the ministry was set up in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me flip it around to the other end. You as a brigade commander become aware of a disciplinary breach by your immediate subordinate. Your immediate subordinates were those company commanders or did you have detachments under you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: The company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If a company commander had committed a breach, refused to obey an order of yours, was the only thing you could do was report him to the chief of the SUP? You couldn't take any disciplinary action yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: To the chief of the SUP or chief of the department of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That last answer got translated as "chief of the department of the interior." I'm not sure what that is. Chief of the Ministry of the Interior or chief of the department of public security? I'm not sure what you're referring to there.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the chief of the department of the police or of the interior in the Secretariat of the Interior where the company commander came from, the OUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: So in the chain of command, that person was lower than the chief of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now related to this I'd like to show you another exhibit. This is P132 in evidence. It's tab 12 in your binder. I think it's the one right in front of what you're looking at now. And you'll see this is the next day, the 19th of June, 1998. It's from General Djordjevic to the various chiefs of the SUP. And it also says to the commander, command of the 24th Detachment of the PJP. That's you; right? I'm sorry, are you finding tab 12?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet. I'm sorry. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you see the people it's addressed to, one of them is to the commander, command of the 24th Detachment; that's you, right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall seeing -- receiving this document in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a long time has passed and there's no reason for me not to believe that I saw it, so I probably saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it looks like you were supposed to see it. Do you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's about the decision to form the 124th. The first sentence says: "In accordance with the proposal made by the commander of the special police units, we hereby attach the decision by the minister to form the 124th ..." Do you know who the commander of the special police units was that's referred to here in the document? Who was that person in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the special police units was, ever since their inception, General Obrad Stevanovic to the best of my knowledge. He held the position until such time as he took up a different position. I think that was the position of the assistant minister. I am not certain, though, of the position he assumed. I only know that he changed positions. Whether he had any say in this or participated in this, I can't tell you because the post that I held at the time would not allow me to have that sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who took Obrad Stevanovic's place as commander of the special police when he moved on to another position? Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when that happened, that Obrad Stevanovic moved from his position as commander of special police units? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly 1996 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then I'm confused because you said for this document issued 19 June 1998 that Obrad Stevanovic was the commander of special police units. So was he still in that position in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you don't know who was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during 1998 and 1999 when you were commander of the 124th Intervention Brigade of the PJP, you didn't know who the commander of the special police units was in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Obrad Stevanovic was present in all the duties involving uniformed police, both regular and extraordinary duties. Now, did -- whether he appeared there as the commander of the PJP or as assistant minister or as something else, I really can't tell. He was present where duties involving the uniformed police were involved. Did I perceive him as the commander at the time? It's quite possible, yes. However, what formally the case was based on the documents, apparently he was not the commander formally at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What document are you referring to that makes you think that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is my opinion because, as I said, in 1996 or 1997 he was appointed assistant minister. This was general knowledge. The only thing is I don't know exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you think that when he became an assistant minister he no longer commanded the special police? Is it possible that he had both jobs?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was quite patient. The witness provided his explanation, and we are going back to the same question for the second or third time and this has led us to an opinion now. He said, I believe that he became assistant minister at such and such a date. I don't want to repeat what the witness said. And now we've come -- we've gone back to the realm of opinions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. -- General Brakovic, do you know of any reason why Obrad Stevanovic taking up the position as an assistant minister would prevent him from continuing to be the commander of the special police units?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the question relates to something that went beyond the post I held and the possibility I had of obtaining information. Could he have? Well, a PJP commander had to have been appointed to that post and perform his duties on the basis of that appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, before you told us that you had been the commander of the 24th Detachment and when it grew in size and became the 124th Intervention Brigade you said you remained the commander and that there wasn't - I understood it - anything done differently to appoint you commander of this new unit. You just stayed in place. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Look at this document that you have in front of you. Paragraph 2 talks about: "In accordance with item 5 of the decision based on individual establishment and criteria for PJP recruitment, the selection of employees and members of the reserve component shall be carried out" and it says "with the prior approval or on the recommendation of the appropriate PJP establishment officers as follows ..." And then it says: "Commander and deputy commander of the intervention brigade with the approval of the PJP commander ..." So who was the PJP commander who approved you as being commander of the intervention brigade? Somebody must have done that, and you don't know who it was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: The text you've just read out "with the prior approval or on the recommendation of the appropriate PJP establishment officers as follows: Commander and deputy commander of the intervention brigade with the approval of the PJP commander." According to this, it was not down to me to seek approval but the chief of the -- it was up to the chief of the secretariat. I told you who it was who nominated me. That's the way things worked. Just as the appointment of the commander and deputy commander of a company is done with the approval of the commander of the intervention brigade, likewise it wasn't up to me to select the commander and deputy commander of the company it was up to the chief of the secretariat. I was only asked an opinion as to whether I agreed that Rade Jankovic should be appointed to such and such a post. I could either say that I agreed or disagreed. In this instant case, I'm not sure, but I assume that it was the chief of the secretariat who nominated me. He must have consulted someone as is stated in this text. I can't tell you who it was because I wasn't there, and he must have sought approval for my appointment. Let me tell you what my understanding of this process was. The chief of the secretariat held a meeting with me when I was nominated to be the commander of the 24th PJP Detachment. When the 24th Detachment became the 124th Intervention Brigade, there were no subsequent discussions. It simply played out by inertia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The 124th Intervention Brigade consisting of eight PJP companies in June 1998 and in 1999, approximately how many men did that have at its largest contingency during that time? Did you have a thousand men?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the precise figure. Approximately up to a thousand at the most. The most precise figure would be around 950. Since I'm not certain, let's allow for the possibility that it was a bit over 950 but not more than a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo we've seen that there were PJP detachments, both some that were from Kosovo and some PJP detachments that were sent in from outside Kosovo, from Serbia proper. What was the size of these detachments approximately? Smaller than a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija, if my memory serves me well, there were four detachments present there and there was the 122nd Intervention Brigade. The detachments had some 150 to 200 men -- fewer men than my detachment, and I think that the 122nd Brigade had the same strength as the 124th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The brigades were clearly the largest group of PJP. So you and the 122nd -- you and the commander of the 122nd were the commanders of the largest contingencies of PJPs in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: If we compared the strengths of the respective units and the differences, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I've heard this term used regarding work in the MUP and it talks about lines of work, and I'm trying to understand this in relation to the hierarchy and the chain of command in the MUP. In your police station in Pristina, you as head of the police department were subordinate to the chief of the police or the chief of the SUP in Pristina. Right so far?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, I was the chief of the police department and my superior was the chief of the secretariat or of the SUP for short.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: SUP stands for the Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I've heard other witnesses from the MUP talk about, for example, within the secretariat you said I think there were, like, 13 department heads. So there was a head of crime police, there was probably a head of administration. You had these other departments within the SUP; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And all 13 of you were subordinate to the chief of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I understood that the department heads also had a line of work where you reported or dealt with your -- your kind of work with somebody at headquarters in the MUP; is that correct? So there would be somebody in the MUP who was responsible for the work of the crime police, and the department head in Pristina for the crime police would report to that person as well as to the chief of the SUP. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the question is beyond the scope of the examination, and I don't think that Mr. Hannis should lead the witness by presenting his own views or conclusions. I think that the direct examination has now turned into viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the witness is a very senior officer. Mr. Hannis would have no prospect of imposing his wishes and thoughts on the witness. There is at times some difficulty in directing the witness's attention to particular issues. I think the form of questioning being used is one that in the circumstances is appropriate and is not likely to lead to any improper or false or misleading evidence. Carry on, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I don't know if you remember my question or understood it, or should I try and ask it again?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I remember it very well. All the communication in the specific case you mentioned between the chief of the crime police department and the police administration went through the chief of the secretariat, and I'm referring to the official communication. Based on my experience, I can tell you that I don't know that I ever spoke directly to the chief of the police department who was my superior along the line that you suggested in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned in your statement - talking about the uniforms and the insignia that the PJP wore -- I wanted to ask you about ribbons that the PJP wore when they were in the field on certain kinds of combat activities. You mentioned in paragraph 8 that they would wear ribbons. I would like to show you 65 ter number 1191. I think that's tab 7 in your binder. If you could have a look at that, please. Have you seen that or something like that before? It's instructions to the police for wearing identification bands in May 1999 from the secretariat in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: You are right. I may have seen that. However, as far as I can see, it was not the Pristina secretariat who sent this or asked for this, it was in the Pristina secretariat that this happened, but I'm familiar with it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the PJP wear armbands, as suggested here in this schedule?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, just as the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could look at the next -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender that one, if I may, 1191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before that happens, perhaps the witness could help me with the notation at the very bottom which appears to be a remark: The army "do not have identification bands." Is that saying that these identification bands were only used by the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read what the document says there at the bottom. However, based on my knowledge dating from that period, I believe that the army definitely had the same identification bands as the police. This was the way in which members of the police and members of the army could recognise one another out in the field in order not to cause friendly fire. What lies behind this remark at the bottom is something I cannot remember at this point. My memory of the events of the time tells me that they did have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00761, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, if you could look at the next tabbed item, number 8, which is 04076 is the 65 ter number. You'll see that's dated the 13th of April from General Lukic, as head of the MUP staff, regarding armbands for the policemen. And it has a chart showing which colours should be worn on which arms on which date. Have you seen that document before, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall this document, though I suppose I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you'll see I think -- it's my third page of that document, there's a list and it lists various SUPs and various PJP detachments and the number of -- the number of individual policemen. And I guess it's a list for how many armbands need to be distributed to those various units. I see the 124th is not included on this list. Would your -- would members of your brigade have been included within the individual SUPs? Is that why the 124th doesn't appear here separately or do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: The only logical reason would be precisely the one that you've stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the next page may help us understand that. It's dated the 26th of May, 1999, from General Lukic and the addressees include not only the secretariats but also the intervention brigade, the 122nd and 124th. And this is with instructions for what ribbons to wear in I think June/July of 1999. Do you recall seeing this document or one like it in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: As with the previous one, I don't recall seeing it, which doesn't rule out the possibility that I did. It's just that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. It was a long time ago. But you have no reason to think that this is not an authentic document. It looks regular in form and you know these kind of orders or instructions were being issued at that time; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't doubt the authenticity of the document at all. I'm merely saying that I can't be sure whether I saw this document while I was reviewing other documents. I do remember seeing similar documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Understand I wasn't challenging you. I was just trying to make sure that this looked to be regular in form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with that, Your Honour, I would tender 4076.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00762, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, one of the reasons that the PJP was wearing these ribbons out in the field was not only to avoid friendly fire but was it also because sometimes the KLA were wearing police or VJ uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO BRAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to go to a new topic. I wonder if this might be an appropriate point to have recess for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you give any indication, Mr. Hannis, of how long you will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I will take another hour and a half, if I may have that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My worry then is whether the evidence of the witness will finish tomorrow, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. I know that's a problem for him. I will do my best to cut down what I'm going to ask him, try to go faster tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We must adjourn overnight now. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. The court officer will give you further instructions. We adjourn now for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
